edition: Issue 029: one lap so good it was illegal, one beach closed to traffic so the pipi can come back, and one Taika film that one-legged its way to two stars
tagline: Your 3-minute Labour Weekend reset. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: Track limits rob Liam Lawson of his best lap as the Kiwi goes 10th in Austin practice
stories.summary: Liam Lawson went 10th fastest in US Grand Prix practice at Austin - and could have been 9th if officials hadn't deleted his best lap for track limits, the same rule that wiped Max Verstappen's headline time.

body.text: Liam Lawson has made a solid start to his United States Grand Prix weekend, going 10th fastest in opening practice at Austin's Circuit of the Americas - on the same day Racing Bulls unveiled what is likely their final major upgrade of the year, with new front and rear wings, floor and engine cover on the VCARB03. His best counted lap of 1m 37.309s was about 1.2 seconds off session leader Charles Leclerc's 1m 36.052s, but Lawson could have finished 9th: a lap of 1m 37.048s was deleted for exceeding track limits. He wasn't alone. Max Verstappen also had a time struck from the sheets after running wide at Turn 19 - a lap that would have been fastest of all. Teammate Arvid Lindblad was 9th, a quarter-second ahead, but faces a grid penalty for exceeding his season's allocation of internal combustion engines. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli was 5th and can wrap up the 2026 title this weekend if he leads the championship by at least 125 points after Monday's race.

Track limits remain the only rulebook in world sport that can confiscate a lap for being too good. On Friday in Austin, a white line ate Max Verstappen's fastest time and then ate Liam Lawson's as well - the motorsport equivalent of being pinged for speeding while parked. As for the second great Austin tradition, the paddock rumour mill: Spanish media reportedly have Lawson replaced by a Bulgarian teenager by breakfast, while the Herald's sources insist everyone's staying put. One deleted lap is not a career verdict - the sport's four-time champion went home with the same fine print. Keep the pace up, Liam. Just keep the tyres off the paint.

NZ Herald (Alex Powell, 23 Oct 2026) reported Lawson finished 10th in US GP FP1 with a best counted lap of 1m 37.309s, about 1.2s off the fastest time, and that a 1m 37.048s lap was deleted for exceeding track limits; Racing Bulls ran four new components (front and rear wings, floor, engine cover); Lindblad was 9th but grid-penalised for exceeding his season's internal combustion engine allocation; Antonelli was 5th and can clinch the title if he leads by 125 points or more after the race. Speedcafe (24 Oct 2026) confirmed Leclerc topped the session at 1m 36.052s - 0.084s clear of Verstappen, whose faster 1m 35.860s was deleted for track limits at Turn 19 - and that Hadjar, Bearman and Ocon also lost laps to track limits.

stories.headline: Kāwhia trust blocks vehicles from the beach to save the kaimoana - and the council says the poles break its bylaw
stories.summary: The Onepū Charitable Trust is blocking vehicles from Kāwhia Beach from Labour Weekend Saturday to save the kaimoana - telling the council, which says the poles breach its traffic bylaw, that it is not taking them down.

body.text: A Waikato coastal trust is putting up a line of two-metre wooden poles at Kāwhia Beach near Maketū marae that will permanently block vehicle access from the Saturday of Labour Weekend. Chair Horahaere Daisy Scott's reason is blunt: the vehicles and motorbikes have ruined our kaimoana beds. Kaumatua Merv Ranga, 74, says the marae used to gather about a dozen sacks of pipi for gatherings; the pipi are dying, and the butterfish, oysters and flounder have gone - it used to take about 30 minutes to get two litres of whitebait, and now there's nothing. A petition signed by 600 people last year, asking the council for an alternative route to Ocean Beach, is still unanswered, so the trust decided to act itself. There's a catch: Ōtorohanga District Council says private landowners can only lawfully block access above high tide, so the poles below the tideline breach its Traffic Management Bylaw. The council asked the trust to remove them. The trust declined. The lagoon itself stays open to walkers and horses.

Every Labour Weekend, New Zealand resumes a proud national tradition: getting into a vehicle to drive to the beach and stand very close to the water. The complication in Kāwhia is that the route happens to run straight through the seafood section - pipi beds, flounder spawning grounds, shorebird nests - and the seafood has been voting with its absence. So the trust put up the world's most polite car-park gate, the council said the posts are technically four metres too far down the beach and therefore illegal, and the trust said thanks but no. When the official answer to 'the dinner is disappearing' is 'the fence is in the wrong tide zone', you know which side is having the better long weekend. To the pipi: you're welcome. To the utes: the beach is still there. It's just become a walking beach, like it's 1840.

RNZ (Rachel Moore, 23 Oct 2026): the Onepū Charitable Trust is installing a two-metre wooden pole barrier at Kāwhia Beach near Maketū marae, closing the gap for vehicles from Labour Weekend Saturday, citing vehicles and motorbikes destroying kaimoana beds (pipi, butterfish, oysters, flounder, whitebait); kaumatua Merv Ranga said the marae used to gather about a dozen sacks of pipi and whitebait took about 30 minutes to collect two litres; chair Horahaere Daisy Scott said the pātaka kai is their inheritance and the trust had had enough of being treated as though local knowledge doesn't matter; a 600-signature petition for an alternative route was lodged last year; Ōtorohanga District Council regulatory and growth manager Tony Quickfall said poles below the tideline breach the council's Traffic Management Bylaw (vehicles restricted to 20kph below high tide) and the council asked the trust to remove them, but the trust declined; the lagoon remains open to walkers and horses.

stories.headline: RNZ review: Klara and the Sun is 'almost certainly' Taika Waititi's worst film
stories.summary: RNZ's reviewer gives Taika Waititi's Klara and the Sun two stars and calls it 'almost certainly' his worst film - while conceding it is handsome and delightfully, unapologetically filmed in New Zealand.

body.text: The verdict is in on Klara and the Sun, Taika Waititi's big-budget adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro's 2021 novel, and RNZ's reviewer has not held back: it is, Boris Jancic writes, almost certainly the worst film a great director - one of New Zealand's greatest ever - has made. The near-future story follows Klara, a teenage-shaped android bought to be a companion to a sick daughter, with Jenna Ortega in the lead, Amy Adams and Natasha Lyonne alongside, and Rachel House in the cast. The two-star review describes the film as manipulated and twee, its comedy scattergun, its final chapters so unearned they feel like the emotional version of a mugging. It also concedes the film is handsome, with genuinely fun retro-futurist sets and costumes, and that there's a certain delight in how unapologetically filmed-in-New-Zealand much of it looks. Jancic notes a tonal shift from the novel is fine in itself - Waititi told RNZ this week that a film and a book are different things - and points out the director has carried that trick off before, in Jojo Rabbit.

Here's the thing about loving Taika Waititi: we all get an opinion on his films, and the national review this week is essentially 'mate. Mate.' He was handed an Ishiguro novel - a loaded gun, artistically speaking - and chose to fire it at the moon with a robot doing a one-legged bit roughly six times. But look on the bright side. The sets are gorgeous, you can practically smell the Waitakere trees, and every Kiwi at the Labour Weekend barbecue will still claim him as ours - usually right after loudly quoting the two-star review. Great directors are allowed a long-weekend flop. Ishiguro's novel will survive. Taika will survive. The one-legged robot is a minor casualty.

RNZ review by Boris Jancic (23 Oct 2026): Klara and the Sun, Taika Waititi's adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro's 2021 novel, rated 2 out of 5 and called almost certainly Waititi's worst film; stars Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Natasha Lyonne, Mia Tharia and Rachel House; the critic calls the comedy scattergun and the finale unearned ('the emotional version of a mugging'), while praising the retro-futurist sets and costumes, the moments the comedy lands, and how unapologetically filmed-in-New-Zealand it looks. The review also notes Waititi told RNZ this week that a film and a book are different things and a change of tone is fine in principle, citing Jojo Rabbit (2019) as a prior tonal success.
